# Lactate transporter MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells promotes fibrotic collagen expression in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis ## Authors - Kyounghee Min1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-2546-0236](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2546-0236)) - Batuhan Yenilmez1 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-8798-3676](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8798-3676)) - Mark Kelly1 - Dimas Echeverria2 - Michael Elleby1 - Lawrence M Lifshitz1 - Naideline Raymond1 - Emmanouela Tsagkaraki1 - Shauna M Harney1 - Chloe DiMarzio1 - Hui Wang1 - Nicholas McHugh2 - Brianna Bramato2 - Brett Morrison3 - Jeffery D Rothstein3 - Anastasia Khvorova2 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-6928-8071](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6928-8071)) - Michael P Czech1 ([ORCID: 0000-0003-4075-7350](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4075-7350)) † ### Affiliations 1. RNA Therapeutics Institute, University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School Worcester United States ([ROR:0464eyp60](https://ror.org/0464eyp60)) 3. Department of Neurology, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Baltimore United States ([ROR:00za53h95](https://ror.org/00za53h95)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Circulating lactate is a fuel source for liver metabolism but may exacerbate metabolic diseases such as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Indeed, haploinsufficiency of lactate transporter monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) in mice reportedly promotes resistance to hepatic steatosis and inflammation. Here, we used adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors to deliver thyroxin binding globulin (TBG)-Cre or lecithin-retinol acyltransferase (Lrat)-Cre to MCT1fl/fl mice on a choline-deficient, high-fat NASH diet to deplete hepatocyte or stellate cell MCT1, respectively. Stellate cell MCT1KO (AAV-Lrat-Cre) attenuated liver type 1 collagen protein expression and caused a downward trend in trichrome staining. MCT1 depletion in cultured human LX2 stellate cells also diminished collagen 1 protein expression. Tetra-ethylenglycol-cholesterol (Chol)-conjugated siRNAs, which enter all hepatic cell types, and hepatocyte-selective tri-N-acetyl galactosamine (GN)-conjugated siRNAs were then used to evaluate MCT1 function in a genetically obese NASH mouse model. MCT1 silencing by Chol-siRNA decreased liver collagen 1 levels, while hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion by AAV-TBG-Cre or by GN-siRNA unexpectedly increased collagen 1 and total fibrosis without effect on triglyceride accumulation. These findings demonstrate that stellate cell lactate transporter MCT1 significantly contributes to liver fibrosis through increased collagen 1 protein expression in vitro and in vivo, while hepatocyte MCT1 appears not to be an attractive therapeutic target for NASH. ## Introduction Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common chronic liver disease, afflicting over a quarter of the world’s population. It describes a spectrum of liver diseases ranging from simple steatosis to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) (Younossi et al., 2016; Estes et al., 2018). Steatosis is considered relatively benign as lifestyle modifications can reverse fatty liver to a healthy condition. On the other hand, NASH is characterized by severe steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis. Severe fibrotic stages of NASH can develop into permanent liver damage, and the disease can progress to cirrhosis and hepatoma. Currently, NASH is a leading cause for liver transplantation, and there is no FDA-approved therapeutic for NASH (Estes et al., 2018; Alexander et al., 2019; Diehl and Day, 2017; Friedman et al., 2018). Since NASH is closely associated with the hallmarks of type 2 diabetes and obesity, including chronic overnutrition, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia, it is likely that substrate overload to the liver contributes to its cause (Friedman et al., 2018). Accordingly, NAFLD and NASH patients display hyperactive liver tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle flux due to an overabundance of upstream metabolites (García-Ruiz and Fernández-Checa, 2018; Sunny et al., 2017). These findings suggest that lowering substrate influx to the liver is a promising strategy to prevent and possibly alleviate steatosis and NASH. Human subjects with type 2 diabetes and obesity reportedly have increased plasma lactate levels (Lovejoy et al., 1992; Crawford et al., 2010; Juraschek et al., 2013a; Juraschek et al., 2013b; DiGirolamo et al., 1992; Sabater et al., 2014; Jansson et al., 1994). Lactate is produced and released into the circulation when cellular glycolytic flux surpasses mitochondrial oxidative capacity. Once considered to be simply a metabolic waste product, lactate is now recognized as a primary fuel for the TCA cycle in liver and thus an essential energy source (Hui et al., 2017; Rabinowitz and Enerbäck, 2020). Additionally, it is a critical regulator that contributes to whole-body energy homeostasis (Brooks, 2020; Li et al., 2022). Under physiological conditions, cellular lactate levels are tightly controlled by monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs). MCTs are members of the solute carrier 16A (SLC16A) family, which are proton-coupled transmembrane protein transporters. Among 14 MCT isoforms, only MCTs 1–4 have been shown to transport monocarboxylate molecules such as lactate, pyruvate, short-chain fatty acids, and ketone bodies (Felmlee et al., 2020). Notably, MCT1 is denoted as a primary lactate transporter as it is the most widely distributed MCT isoform in various metabolic tissues and has a high affinity for lactate, maintaining basal cellular homeostasis according to transmembrane lactate gradients (Li et al., 2022; Halestrap, 2013). Reportedly, MCT1 haploinsufficiency in mice reduces MCT1 protein levels to nearly half in major metabolic tissues such as liver, brain, and white adipose tissues, and these mice are resistant to diet-induced obesity and liver steatosis and inflammation (Lengacher et al., 2013; Carneiro et al., 2017; Hadjihambi et al., 2023). The role of MCT1 in hypothalamus and adipose tissues in these phenotypes was ruled out, as selective MCT1 depletion in those tissues either increased food intake and body weight (Elizondo-Vega et al., 2016) or enhanced systemic inflammation and insulin resistance (Lin et al., 2022). Thus, the question of which tissue or tissues are responsible for the phenotype of whole-body MCT1 haploinsufficiency is not solved. The above considerations suggest the possibility that MCT1KO in one or more liver cell types may explain the effects of MCT1 haploinsufficiency in mice. Since hepatocytes account for the majority of liver cells and have high rates of lipogenesis and triglyceride (TG) accumulation, lactate levels governed by hepatocyte MCT1 could be involved in regulating steatosis. On the other hand, while hepatic stellate cells account for only 5–10% of the hepatic cell population, they are the major cell type contributing to hepatic fibrogenesis (Wake, 1971; Mederacke et al., 2013). Fate tracing studies have revealed that 82–96% of myofibroblasts are derived from hepatic stellate cells, which are liver-specific pericytes (Mederacke et al., 2013). During NASH progression, multiple liver injury signals stimulate the transition of vitamin A-storing quiescent hepatic stellate cells into fibrogenic, proliferative myofibroblasts that produce and secrete collagen fibers (Trautwein et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2015; Puche et al., 2013; Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017). As a result, healthy hepatic parenchyma is replaced with a collagen-rich extracellular matrix, turning the liver into a hardened and scarred tissue (Mehal et al., 2011). In general, major organ fibrosis is directly correlated with morbidity and mortality, contributing up to 45% of deaths in developed countries (Wynn, 2008). Thus, targeting activated hepatic stellate cells has become a major strategy in NASH therapeutics development (Friedman et al., 2018; Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017). However, the role of MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells activation or fibrogenesis has not been investigated. The aim of the present studies was to investigate the role of hepatic lactate transport via MCT1 in lipid metabolism and fibrogenesis in NASH, and to determine its potential suitability as a therapeutic target. Two key unanswered questions were of particular interest: (1) is it hepatocyte-specific MCT1 depletion that protects mice with MCT1 haploinsufficiency from liver lactate overload and NAFLD and (2) does liver stellate cell MCT1 promote hepatic fibrogenesis that occurs in NASH? We tested the possible enhancement of lipogenesis and fat accumulation via MCT1 function specifically in hepatocytes using adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated thyroxin binding globulin (TBG)-Cre MCT1KO in MCT1fl/fl mice, and in other experiments by silencing hepatocyte MCT1 with tri-N-acetyl galactosamine (GN)-conjugated siRNA. These experiments showed that hepatocyte MCT1 loss decreased expression of enzymes in the de novo lipogenesis (DNL) pathway, but did not diminish overall steatosis. Surprisingly, hepatocyte MCT1KO increased liver fibrosis in two mouse models of NASH. In contrast, hepatic stellate cell-selective MCT1KO, achieved by injection of AAV9-lecithin-retinol acyltransferase (Lrat)-Cre into MCT1fl/fl mice, did attenuate collagen production and fibrosis. Our findings underscore the critical importance of implementing cell type-specific targeting strategies to diminish NASH fibrogenesis. ## Results ### MCT1 depletion prevents TGF-β1-stimulated type 1 collagen production in cultured human LX2 stellate cells As fate tracing studies have revealed that 82–96% of myofibroblasts are derived from hepatic stellate cells (Mederacke et al., 2013), we employed a simple in vitro system utilizing LX2 human hepatic stellate cells to investigate effects of MCT1 silencing on expression of type 1 collagen, a major component of fibrosis. Cells were transfected with Lipofectamine and native MCT1-targeting siRNA (MCT1-siRNA), which diminished SLC16A1/MCT1 mRNA expression by about 80% (Figure 1A), or nontargeted control (NTC-siRNA), and then treated with transforming growth factor 1β (TGF-β1) (10 µg/ml) for 48 hr. As expected, TGF-β1 stimulated expression of ACTA2 and collagen 1 isoform, COL1A1, by several folds (Figure 1B and C). SLC16A1/MCT1 silencing significantly inhibited TGF-β1-stimulated ACTA2 mRNA expression as well as collagen 1 protein production (Figure 1B and C), indicating cell-autonomous functions of MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89136/elife-89136-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** Cells were transfected with either NTC-siRNA or MCT1-siRNA for 6 hr. Then, cells were maintained in serum-starved media with or without 10 ng/ml of recombinant human TGF-β1 for 48 hr and harvested. (A) SLC16A1/MCT1 mRNA expression levels. (B) Collagen 1 protein levels. Quantification was added below. (C) Representative fibrogenic marker genes, ACTA2, and COL1A1 expression levels were monitored (mean ± SD, t-test, one-way ANOVA, *: p<0.05, **: p<0.01, ***: p<0.001, ****: p<0.0001). ### Identification of a potent, chemically modified siRNA candidate targeting MCT1 Given the therapeutic potential of SLC16A1/MCT1 silencing in preventing fibrogenesis (Figure 1), we aimed to develop MCT1-siRNA compounds, chemically modified for stability, potency, and delivery in vivo for use in this research and potentially for therapeutic advancement. Asymmetrical siRNA compounds used here are composed of 15 double-strand nucleotides with a short overhanging single-strand that promotes cellular uptake (Behlke, 2006; Khvorova and Watts, 2017). To enhance the stability of the constructs, the 2’-OH of each ribose was modified to either 2’-O-methyl or 2’-fluoro. In addition, phosphorothioate linkage backbone modifications were applied to avoid exonuclease degradation. Tetra-ethylenglycol-cholesterol (Chol) was conjugated to the 3’ end-sense strand to enhance stability and cellular uptake of candidate compounds. We performed in vitro screening to select the most potent Chol-MCT1-siRNA compounds that were initially synthesized (Figure 2A and B). Each Chol-MCT1-siRNA compound candidate was treated into mouse hepatocyte FL83B cells. As opposed to native siRNA, our Chol-MCT1-siRNA does not require transfection reagents as it is fully chemically modified. The silencing effect on Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA was monitored after 72 hr (Figure 2B). Several compounds elicited a silencing effect greater than 80% compared to the Chol-NTC-siRNA. The two most potent Chol-MCT1-siRNA, Chol-MCT1-2060 (IC50: 59.6 nM, KD%: 87.2) and Chol-MCT1-3160 (IC50: 32.4 nM, KD%: 87.7) (Figure 2C), were evaluated for their inhibitory effect on MCT1 protein levels (Figure 2D and E). ### Distinct cellular biodistribution of Chol- vs GN-conjugated siRNAs For in vivo studies, further chemical modifications were applied (Figure 3A). MCT1-siRNAs utilized in in vivo studies are double-strand oligonucleotides comprised of 18 sense and 20 antisense nucleotides. At the 5’-end of the antisense strand, a 5’-(E)-vinyl-phosphonate modification was added to prevent phosphatase-induced degradation, enhancing in vivo stability and promoting its accumulation in target cells. Either a hydrophobic Chol or a hepatocyte-targeting GN was attached to the 3’-end of sense strands of MCT1-siRNAs to direct different hepatic cellular biodistribution. ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89136/elife-89136-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** Male C57BL/6 wild-type mice (16–18 weeks, n=4) were subcutaneously injected with 10 mg/kg of each siRNA, twice within 15 days, while fed a chow diet. To validate the biodistribution of siRNAs with these two conjugates, 10 mg/kg of each siRNA was subcutaneously injected into 16- to 18-week-old male C57BL/6 wild-type mice twice within a 15-day period. On day 15, mice were sacrificed and the livers were perfused to isolate multiple hepatic cell types, including hepatocytes, stellate cells, and Kupffer cells. Isolation of each hepatic cell type was validated for enrichment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F). As expected, GN-conjugated, fully chemically modified MCT1-siRNA (GN-MCT1-siRNA) silenced Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA only in the hepatocyte fraction (Figure 3B–D), as GN binds to the asialoglycoprotein receptor primarily expressed in hepatocytes. On the other hand, Chol-MCT1-siRNA silenced Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA levels in all hepatic cell types (Figure 3E–G), as its cellular uptake is highly dependent on the non-specific, hydrophobic interaction between cholesterol and plasma membranes. Notably, the hepatic stellate cell fraction distinguishes GN-MCT1-siRNA from Chol-MCT1-siRNA in biodistribution, as only the latter silences Slc16a1/Mct1 in stellate cells (Figure 3C vs F). We also confirmed that both GN-MCT1-siRNA and Chol-MCT1-siRNA do not affect MCT1 levels in other major metabolic tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J). ### Subcutaneous injection of Chol-MCT1-siRNA or GN-MCT1-siRNA silences hepatic MCT1 in a genetically obese NASH mouse model We next investigated the effect of Chol-MCT1-siRNA on reversing severe steatosis in the genetically obese ob/ob mouse on a NASH-inducing Gubra Amylin NASH (GAN) diet (Yenilmez et al., 2022). These mice normally develop severe steatosis from an early age but hardly develop fibrosis until fed the GAN diet. Each siRNA (10 mg/kg) was subcutaneously injected once every 10 days and mice were fed a GAN diet for 3 weeks before sacrifice (Figure 4A). Hepatic MCT1 protein levels were visually monitored by MCT1-positive staining immunohistochemistry (Figure 4B and C), showing more than 70% MCT1 protein depletion (Chol-MCT1-siRNA: 77.99% and GN-MCT1-siRNA: 71.35% silencing). Similar silencing was observed when Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA levels were measured by real-time quantitative PCR (rt-qPCR) (Figure 4D). The silencing was Slc16a1/Mct1 selective, not depleting other isoforms such as Slc16a7/Mct2 and Slc16a3/Mct4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B). Importantly, there was no surge in plasma lactate level (Figure 4E), addressing the concern of potential lactic acidosis after MCT1 depletion in the liver, the major lactate-consuming tissue. We also monitored food intake and body weight over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D), as there was a report of decreased food anticipation activity upon hepatic MCT1 deletion followed by reduced plasma β-hydroxybutyrate levels (Martini et al., 2021). Intriguingly, the GN-MCT1-siRNA administration led to a decrease in both food intake and body weight, while the Chol-MCT1-siRNA did not. Neither Chol-MCT1-siRNA administration nor hepatocyte-specific MCT1KO improved glucose tolerance on the genetically obese NASH mouse model or a 12-week HFD-induced NAFLD model, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F). ![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89136/elife-89136-fig4-v1.jpg) **Figure 4.:** (A) Male ob/ob mice (10 weeks, n=6) were subcutaneously injected with 10 mg/kg of siRNA once every 10 days. We also provided evidence that lactate may enhance TGF-β1-induced collagen production via MCT1 in studies in cultured LX2 cells. The finding in mice was made by generating novel AAV9-Lrat-Cre constructs that can be injected into MCT1fl/fl mice to elicit stellate cell-selective MCT1 depletion, as verified by isolation and Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA analysis in liver cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). Previous use of Lrat-Cre for germline transmission had validated constitutive gene KO selectively in hepatic stellate cells in mice (Mederacke et al., 2013), while our AAV-Lrat-Cre construct allows inducible gene KO, eliminating time-demanding mouse crossing and breeding. Surprisingly, MCT1KO in hepatocytes, both in vivo (Figure 7A) and in vitro (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), evoked the opposite effect: a robust upregulation of collagen 1 expression and fibrosis. This may be an effect of increased local lactate to enhance stellate cell collagen production, but may also be in part a cell-autonomous effect in hepatocytes, as we observed increased collagen 1 expression in Hep2G cells upon silencing SLC16A1/MCT1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2). The hepatocyte-selective MCT1KO caused increased total fibrosis, evidenced by trichrome staining of liver (Figure 7D and E), while the stellate cell MCT1KO was associated with a trend toward diminished trichrome staining that did not reach statistical significance (Figure 7D and E). Nonetheless, taken together, our data suggest that lactate flux via MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells strongly promotes collagen 1 translation or inhibits protein turnover rates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3). Interestingly, the inhibitory effect of stellate cell MCT1KO was observed only at the collagen 1 protein level, while the hepatocyte MCT1KO affected both collagen mRNA and protein. The exact mechanism needs to be further investigated, but one possibility is that increased import of lactate into hepatic stellate cells serves as a precursor for glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline synthesis, as suggested in other systems such as cancer or pulmonary fibrosis (Pérez-Escuredo et al., 2016; Hamanaka et al., 2019). This could potentially explain why MCT1 depletion in stellate cells has a greater translational effect on collagen expression rather than transcriptional regulation. Strong support for the above conclusions was obtained in an alternative experimental model of NASH—genetically obese ob/ob mice on a GAN diet (Yenilmez et al., 2022). In these experiments we employed chemically stabilized siRNA, taking advantage of RNA modifications 2-fluoro, 2-O-methyl ribose, and phosphorothioate backbone replacement to block siRNA degradation and immune responses as well as enhance in vivo delivery effectiveness and silencing longevity (Behlke, 2006; Khvorova and Watts, 2017). Conjugation of such siRNA compounds with GN promotes binding to the asialoglycoprotein receptor that is primarily expressed in hepatocytes at high levels, and we confirmed hepatocyte-selective gene silencing with such constructs (Figure 3B–D). Moreover, injection of GN-MCT1-siRNA did not affect MCT1 expression in other major tissues including inguinal white adipose tissue, gonadal white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue, intestine, heart, lung, kidney, and spleen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H). Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 silencing strongly upregulated collagen 1 in livers of ob/ob mice on a GAN diet (Figure 5D–F), as did hepatocyte-selective MCT1KO in the CDHFD mouse model (Figure 7A). In contrast, Chol-conjugated, chemically modified siRNA targeting MCT1 silenced the gene in all three liver cell types tested, including hepatic stellate cells (Figure 3E–G), and did attenuate liver collagen 1 expression (Figure 5A and B). This result is consistent with the idea that depleting MCT1 in stellate cells decreases collagen 1 production, as shown by MCT1KO in stellate cells (Figure 7B). The data in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 also show the effectiveness of RNA interference (RNAi) in interrogating cell-specific processes in liver, and highlight the multiple advantages over traditional small molecule inhibitors in developing therapeutics (Bumcrot et al., 2006; Aagaard and Rossi, 2007). To date, five RNAi-based therapeutic agents have received FDA approvals targeting multiple disease areas, and a great many clinical trials of oligonucleotide therapeutics are in progress (Padda et al., 2023; Traber and Yu, 2023; Zhu et al., 2022; Mullard, 2022). Analysis of gene expression profiles also showed that hepatic MCT1 positively regulates the levels of SREBP1 and ChREBP, major transcription factors regulating liver lipid metabolism, as well as their target DNL genes. These effects were apparently not sufficient to reverse severe steatosis in the genetically obese NASH mouse model (Figure 4), although a slight decrease in mean lipid droplet size was observed. The remaining steatosis may be attributed to the continuous supply of fatty acids from adipose tissue lipolysis, which accounts for up to 65% of hepatic fat accumulation as opposed to only 25% coming from hepatic DNL (Donnelly et al., 2005). While recognizing that the decreased expression of DNL genes does not necessarily indicate an inhibited fatty acid synthesis rate, we also cannot rule out the possibility of compensatory effects from other MCT isoforms that are expressed. However, since MCT1 haploinsufficiency showed greatly reduced HFD-induced hepatic steatosis, the discrepancies with our data may be due to other tissues being involved or the different mouse models used. Overall, it is clear from our studies that steatosis is not much affected by hepatic MCT1 depletion in two models of NASH in mice. A possible future strategy for NASH therapeutics may be to combine the depletion of MCT1 in stellate cells to decrease fibrosis with a potent anti-steatosis target such as DGAT2 (Yenilmez et al., 2022; Calle et al., 2021; Loomba et al., 2020) which we and others have shown is effective in reducing steatosis when depleted. Although there are still remaining challenges in developing a successful hepatic stellate cell-selective delivery system (Poelstra, 2020), ongoing studies are identifying promising candidates such as M6P-polyethylene glycol (Zhu and Mahato, 2010), IGF2R-specific peptide coupled nanocomplex (Zhao et al., 2018), and others (Chen et al., 2019). To understand the underlying mechanism by which hepatic MCT1 depletion drives the downregulation of DNL genes expression, we investigated AMPK activation, as pAMPK has a negative regulatory effect on SREBP1 and ChREBP activation (Li et al., 2011; Kawaguchi et al., 2002). Indeed, hepatic MCT1 silencing enhanced AMPK phosphorylation, consistent with the previous MCT1 haploinsufficient mice study (Carneiro et al., 2017). These data are also in line with another study in which MCT1 inhibition reduced ATP production and activated AMPK, thus deactivating SREBP1c and lowering levels of its target SCD1 (Zhao et al., 2020). It remains to be examined whether other mechanisms are also at play that connect MCT1 function in liver to DNL gene regulation. In summary, the data presented here highlight hepatic stellate cell MCT1 as a potential therapeutic target to prevent NASH fibrogenesis related to collagen 1 production. Its utility as a therapeutic target is complicated by our finding that MCT1 depletion in hepatocytes actually increases fibrosis. This work highlights the importance of contemplating cell-type specificity when developing therapeutic strategies, especially in systems of complex cellular landscapes such as NASH. ## Materials and methods ### Oligonucleotide synthesis The 15–20 or 18–20 sequence oligonucleotides were synthesized by phosphoramidite solid-phase synthesis on a Dr Oligo 48 (Biolytic, Fremont, CA, USA), or MerMade12 (Biosearch Technologies, Novato, CA, USA) using 2ʹ-F and 2ʹ-O-Me phosphoramidites with standard protecting groups (Chemgenes, Wilmington, MA, USA). Synthesis columns containing the oligonucleotides covalently attached to the solid supports were cleaved and deprotected for 1 hr at room temperature with anhydrous mono-methylamine gas (Airgas). ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89136.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89136.3.sa1)

The authors put forth the hypothesis that hepatocyte and/or non-parenchymal liver MCT1 may be responsible for physiologic effects (lower body weight gain and less hepatic steatosis) in MCT1 global heterozygote mice. They generate multiple tools to test this hypothesis, which they combine with mouse diets that induce fatty liver, steatohepatitis and fibrosis. Novel findings include that deletion of hepatocyte MCT1 does not change liver lipid content, but increases liver fibrosis. Deletion of hepatic stellate cell (HSC) MCT1 does not substantially affect any liver parameter, but concomitant HSC MCT1 deletion does reverse fibrosis seen with hepatocyte MCT1 knockout or knockdown. In both models, plasma lactate levels do not change, suggesting that liver MCT1 does not substantially affect systemic lactate. In general, the data match conclusions of the manuscript, and the studies are well-conducted and well-described. Further work would be necessary to dissect mechanism of fibrosis with hepatocyte MCT1, and whether this is due to changes in local lactate (as speculated by the authors) or another MCT1 substrate. This would be important to understand this novel potential cross-talk between hepatocytes and HSCs.

A parallel and perhaps more important advance is the generation of new methodology to target HSC in mice, using modified siRNA and by transduction of AAV9-Lrat-Cre. Both methods would reduce the need to cross floxed mice with the Lrat-Cre allele, saving time and resources. These tools were validated to an extent by the authors, but not sufficiently to ensure that there is no cross-reactivity with other liver cell types. For example, AAV9-Lrat-Cre-transduced MCT1 floxed mice show compelling HSC but not hepatocyte Mct1 knockdown, but other liver cell types should be assessed to ensure specificity. This is particularly important as overall liver Mct1 decreased by ~30% in AAV9-Lrat-Cre-transduced mice, which may exceed HSC content of these mice, especially when considering a 60-70% knockdown efficiency. This same issue also affects Chol-MCT1-siRNA, which the authors demonstrate to affect hepatocytes and HSC, but likely affects other cell types not tested. As this is a new and potentially valuable tool, it would be important to assess Mct1 expression across more non-parenchymal cells (i.e. endothelial, cholangiocytes, immune cells) to determine penetration and efficacy.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89136.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89136.3.sa2)

In this study, the authors seek to answer two main questions: (1) Whether interfering with lactate availability in hepatocytes through depletion of hepatocyte specific MCT-1 depletion would reduce steatosis, and (2) Whether MCT-1 in stellate cells promote fibrogenesis. While the first question is based on the observation that haploinsufficiency of MCT-1 makes mice resistant to steatosis, the rationale behind how MCT-1 could impact fibrogenesis in stellate cells is not clear. A more detailed discussion regarding how lactate availability would regulate two different processes in two different cell types would be helpful. The authors employ several mouse models and in vitro systems to show that MCT1 inhibition in hepatic stellate cells reduces the expression of COL-1.

The authors have sufficiently addressed prior comments and added new experiments to provide details on possible mechanisms.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89136.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89136.3.sa3)

We commend the authors on addressing our points and do believe that the manuscript is much improved. Even with the added in vitro data (Figure 8, Supplementary Figure 6), however, a clear mechanistic explanation for how MCT1 is modulating/inhibiting fibrosis in hepatic stellate cells is lacking and this represents a key area for future exploration. The authors provide interesting follow up experiments that suggest lactate can potentiate TGF-β1 signaling, a phenomenon that has previously been described in pulmonary fibrosis. Additionally, MCT1 depletion decreased the pSMAD3/SMAD ratio, but this was overcome with higher doses of TGB- β1 ligand. It remains unclear how intracellular versus extracellular lactate is signaling to exert the observed effects, and how the altered metabolism/metabolic flux in NAFLD is contributing to organ level metabolic dysregulation. These will be keys questions to answer going forward potentially using the novel in vivo models that the authors have contributed here.

A major finding of this work is that loss of monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1), specifically in stellate cells, can decrease fibrosis in the liver. However, the underlying mechanism whereby MCT1 influences stellate cells is not addressed. It is unclear if upstream/downstream metabolic flux within different cell types leads to fibrotic outcomes. Ultimately, the paper opens more questions than it answers: why does decreasing MCT1 expression in hepatocytes exacerbate disease, while silencing MCT1 in fibroblasts seems to alleviate collagen deposition? Mechanistic studies in isolated hepatocytes and stellate cells could enhance the work further to show the disparate pathways that mediate these opposing effects. The work highlights the complexity of cellular behavior and metabolism within a disease environment but does little to mechanistically explain it.

results.result: MCT1 depletion in cultured human LX2 stellate cells inhibits TGF-β1-stimulated collagen 1 production. SLC16A1/MCT1 silencing significantly reduced both ACTA2 mRNA and collagen 1 protein expression in TGF-β1-treated LX2 cells, indicating cell-autonomous functions of MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C51-C54 provide consistent in vitro evidence from LX2 stellate cells showing that MCT1 silencing inhibits TGF-β1-induced collagen expression at both mRNA and protein levels (Figure 1). The data demonstrate appropriate controls (NTC-siRNA), effective knockdown (~80% reduction in MCT1 mRNA), and statistically significant effects on fibrogenic markers. The conclusion of cell-autonomous function is appropriately drawn from direct manipulation in isolated cells.

results.result: Development and validation of cell-type-selective siRNA constructs targeting MCT1. Chol-MCT1-3160 (IC50: 32.4 nM, 87.7% knockdown) was selected for in vivo studies. GN-conjugated siRNA silenced MCT1 only in hepatocytes, while Chol-conjugated siRNA silenced MCT1 in all hepatic cell types including stellate cells, with no off-target effects in other metabolic tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C63 describe comprehensive validation of siRNA constructs with appropriate dose-response curves (Figure 2C), cell-type-specific biodistribution confirmed by isolating and analyzing hepatocytes, stellate cells, and Kupffer cells (Figure 3), and verification of tissue specificity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The differential targeting is mechanistically explained by receptor specificity (asialoglycoprotein receptor for GN) versus non-specific membrane interactions (cholesterol). This represents rigorous methodological development essential for subsequent experiments.

results.result: Pan-hepatic MCT1 silencing by Chol-siRNA decreases liver collagen 1 levels in obese NASH mice. Chol-MCT1-siRNA administration to ob/ob mice on GAN diet significantly reduced liver collagen 1 protein levels, consistent with in vitro LX2 cell data.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C80, C131-C132 demonstrate that Chol-siRNA (which targets all hepatic cell types including stellate cells) reduces collagen 1 protein in vivo (Figures 5A-B). The effect is statistically significant and consistent with the in vitro stellate cell data (C6). The ~78% MCT1 knockdown was confirmed by IHC (C65), and the siRNA was selective for MCT1 without affecting other MCT isoforms (C67). The result is internally consistent across two experimental systems.

results.result: Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion unexpectedly increases collagen 1 expression and fibrosis in NASH mice. Both AAV-TBG-Cre and GN-siRNA approaches to deplete MCT1 specifically in hepatocytes resulted in increased collagen 1 at mRNA and protein levels, and enhanced Sirius Red-positive fibrotic areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C82-C84, C130 present a surprising and well-replicated finding using two independent methods (AAV-TBG-Cre and GN-siRNA) in two different NASH models (ob/ob+GAN and CDHFD). The hepatocyte-specific targeting was validated by cell fractionation (C58, C89), and the pro-fibrotic effect was observed at both mRNA and protein levels (C82-C83) with increased Sirius Red staining (C84). The consistency across methods and models strongly supports this counterintuitive result.

results.result: Stellate cell-specific MCT1 knockout attenuates collagen 1 expression and shows a downward trend in fibrosis. AAV-Lrat-Cre-mediated MCT1 deletion specifically in hepatic stellate cells reduced CDHFD-induced collagen 1 protein levels and showed a downward trend in trichrome staining.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C88-C90, C95, C98 demonstrate stellate cell-specific MCT1 knockout using a novel AAV-Lrat-Cre construct with appropriate validation of cell-type specificity (C88-C90). While collagen 1 protein reduction was statistically significant (C95, Figure 7B), the trichrome staining showed only a downward trend without reaching statistical significance (C5, C98, Figure 7D-E). This discrepancy between collagen 1 protein and total fibrosis measures creates uncertainty about the overall anti-fibrotic effect, though the direction is consistent with the Chol-siRNA results.

results.result: Hepatocyte-specific MCT1 knockout accelerates fibrosis in the CDHFD NASH model. Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 deletion by AAV-TBG-Cre enhanced collagen 1 levels, accelerated trichrome-detected fibrosis, and increased liver stiffness at 4 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claims C94, C97, C100, C124 provide convergent evidence from multiple fibrosis measures (collagen 1 protein, trichrome staining, liver stiffness by SWE) that hepatocyte MCT1 knockout worsens fibrosis (Figure 7A, D-G). This replicates the GN-siRNA findings (C10-C11, C82-C84) using an independent genetic approach in a different NASH model, strengthening the conclusion. The liver stiffness data (C100) provides functional validation of the histological findings.

results.result: Dual MCT1 knockout in both hepatocytes and stellate cells produces intermediate effects on fibrosis. Combined deletion of MCT1 in both cell types blunted the individual effects and showed no significant change in overall fibrosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C96, C99 demonstrate that simultaneous knockout in both cell types produces an intermediate phenotype (Figure 7C, D-E), consistent with opposing effects of MCT1 in the two cell types. This result is internally consistent with the individual knockout experiments and provides important evidence that the cell-type-specific effects are genuine and can counteract each other. The statistical analysis appears appropriate for the observed data.

results.result: Hepatic MCT1 depletion does not significantly reduce steatosis in NASH models. Neither GN-MCT1-siRNA nor Chol-MCT1-siRNA decreased total hepatic triglyceride levels in ob/ob mice on GAN diet, and MCT1 deletion in either hepatocytes or stellate cells did not resolve steatosis in the CDHFD model, despite small changes in lipid droplet morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74, C93, C136, C139 consistently show that MCT1 depletion, regardless of cell-type specificity or method, does not substantially affect steatosis across two NASH models (Figures 4H, 6E-F). While subtle morphological changes in lipid droplets were observed (C73-C74), total triglyceride content remained unchanged. This negative result is important and well-documented, though the authors appropriately note limitations in interpreting the lack of effect on steatosis given the complex etiology involving adipose tissue lipolysis (C137).

results.result: Hepatic MCT1 depletion downregulates de novo lipogenesis genes and activates AMPK. Both GN-MCT1-siRNA and Chol-MCT1-siRNA decreased mRNA and protein levels of DNL genes (SREBP1, ChREBP, FASN, SCD1, ACLY) and increased AMPK phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76, C79, C135, C141 demonstrate consistent downregulation of lipogenic transcription factors and their target genes with both siRNA approaches (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The mechanistic link through AMPK activation is supported by increased pAMPK levels (C79) and is consistent with prior literature (C77-C78, C142). However, these molecular changes did not translate to reduced steatosis (C136), suggesting compensatory mechanisms or that DNL is not the primary driver of steatosis in these models.

results.result: Lactate enhances TGF-β1-induced collagen production via MCT1 in stellate cells. Lactate alone did not induce collagen expression, but the combination of lactate and pyruvate significantly enhanced TGF-β1-stimulated collagen 1 production in LX2 cells, and this effect was prevented by MCT1 depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C108, C121 provide mechanistic insight through dose-response experiments (Figure 8A-B) and combination treatments (Figure 8C-E). The data show that lactate acts as a co-factor rather than a primary inducer, requiring both TGF-β1 and pyruvate for maximal effect. MCT1 depletion blocked collagen production under both endogenous and exogenous lactate conditions (C106-C107, Figure 8F-G), demonstrating that lactate transport is necessary for the effect. The experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis with relevant controls.

results.result: MCT1 regulates collagen production through both SMAD3-dependent and independent pathways. MCT1 depletion decreased pSMAD3 levels in the absence of TGF-β1, but this effect was limited at higher TGF-β1 concentrations, suggesting involvement of both SMAD3-dependent and independent mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 present mechanistic data on SMAD3 signaling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), but the results are complex and somewhat inconsistent. While MCT1 depletion reduced pSMAD3 in basal conditions (C109), the effect was concentration-dependent and diminished at higher TGF-β1 levels (C111-C112). The authors appropriately acknowledge that both SMAD3-dependent and independent pathways may be involved (C113), but the relative contributions remain unclear. Additional experiments would be needed to definitively establish the mechanism, making this result uncertain rather than fully supported.

results.result: MCT1 depletion in hepatocytes directly increases fibrogenic gene expression. MCT1 silencing in HepG2 hepatocytes enhanced ACTA2 and COL1A1 expression, but conditioned media from these cells did not affect fibrogenic gene expression in LX2 stellate cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 provide evidence for a cell-autonomous effect of hepatocyte MCT1 depletion on fibrogenic gene expression (Figure 8—figure supplement 2). The conditioned media experiment (C117) appropriately tests whether the effect is mediated by secreted factors, and the negative result supports a direct effect. However, the authors appropriately note (C119) that stellate cells are the primary collagen producers, so the physiological significance of hepatocyte collagen expression remains unclear. The data support the conclusion but highlight the complexity of the system.

results.result: The opposite fibrotic effects of GN-MCT1-siRNA versus Chol-MCT1-siRNA are not due to differential M1/M2 macrophage polarization. Both siRNA treatments produced comparable M1 and M2 macrophage marker expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 address an important alternative hypothesis about macrophage polarization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The data show no significant differences in M1/M2 markers between the two siRNA treatments, appropriately ruling out this mechanism. This negative result is valuable for interpretation and helps focus attention on the direct effects in hepatocytes and stellate cells. The experimental design and analysis are appropriate for testing this hypothesis.

results.result: Both Chol-MCT1-siRNA and GN-MCT1-siRNA achieve >70% MCT1 knockdown in ob/ob mice without causing lactic acidosis or affecting other MCT isoforms. Hepatic MCT1 protein was reduced by ~78% (Chol) and ~71% (GN) with selective targeting of MCT1 and no increase in plasma lactate.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 provide essential validation data for the in vivo experiments (Figure 4B-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B). The knockdown efficiency was confirmed by both IHC and qPCR, selectivity for MCT1 over other isoforms was demonstrated, and the absence of lactic acidosis addresses a key safety concern. These data establish that the experimental manipulations were effective and specific, supporting the validity of downstream phenotypic analyses.

results.result: GN-MCT1-siRNA, but not Chol-MCT1-siRNA, decreased food intake and body weight in ob/ob mice on GAN diet. This differential effect suggests hepatocyte-specific MCT1 depletion influences feeding behavior or energy balance.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 identify a differential metabolic effect between the two siRNA approaches (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D). The observation is clearly documented and statistically significant. However, the mechanism is not explored, and the relationship to the fibrosis phenotype is unclear. The authors appropriately note this as an intriguing finding without over-interpreting it. This represents a well-documented observation that warrants future investigation.

results.result: MCT1 depletion does not improve glucose tolerance in NASH models. Neither Chol-MCT1-siRNA in ob/ob mice nor hepatocyte-specific MCT1KO in HFD-fed mice improved glucose tolerance.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 reports negative results on glucose tolerance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-F) across two models and approaches. While negative, this result is important for understanding the metabolic consequences of MCT1 depletion and is appropriately documented. The data suggest that MCT1's effects on fibrosis are independent of glucose homeostasis, helping to delineate the mechanism.

results.result: Cell-type-specific MCT1 deletion does not affect food intake, body weight, or plasma ALT levels in the CDHFD model. No differences were observed between control, hepatocyte KO, stellate cell KO, or dual KO groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C102 document the absence of effects on basic metabolic parameters and liver injury markers (Figure 6C-D, Figure 7H) in the CDHFD model. These negative results are important controls showing that the fibrotic effects are not secondary to changes in food intake, body weight, or general hepatotoxicity. The data support the specificity of the fibrotic phenotypes observed.

results.result: All groups showed similar liver stiffness after 8 weeks of CDHFD. Despite differences at 4 weeks, liver stiffness converged to similar levels across all groups by 8 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 describes the temporal dynamics of liver stiffness (Figure 7G), showing that early differences (C100) were not maintained at the study endpoint. This result is clearly documented but somewhat difficult to interpret given the persistent differences in collagen 1 and trichrome staining at 8 weeks. The discrepancy between stiffness and histological measures may reflect technical limitations of SWE or biological complexity in the relationship between collagen deposition and tissue mechanics.

results.result: Stellate cell MCT1 promotes liver fibrosis while hepatocyte MCT1 appears protective, highlighting the importance of cell-type-specific targeting in NASH therapeutics. MCT1 in stellate cells contributes to collagen 1 production, but hepatocyte MCT1 depletion increases fibrosis, complicating therapeutic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14, C120, C143-C145 represent the major conclusions synthesizing results from multiple experimental approaches (in vitro LX2 cells, two in vivo NASH models, two targeting methods). The opposing effects in different cell types are consistently demonstrated across experiments. The conclusion about therapeutic implications (C143-C144) is appropriately cautious given the complexity. The emphasis on cell-type specificity (C145) is well-supported and represents an important conceptual advance for the field.

results.result: MCT1 depletion in hepatic stellate cells reduces collagen 1 expression and fibrosis. This was demonstrated in vitro using LX2 stellate cells where MCT1 silencing inhibited TGF-β1-stimulated collagen 1 production, and in vivo using AAV-Lrat-Cre-mediated stellate cell-specific MCT1 knockout in mice on CDHFD, which attenuated collagen 1 protein levels and showed a downward trend in trichrome staining.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as a major finding, stating 'A major finding of this work is that loss of monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1), specifically in stellate cells, can decrease fibrosis in the liver.' The editor describes the manuscript as 'convincing' and representing 'a valuable advance in understanding the role of MCT1.' Reviewer 1 notes the 'novel findings' and states 'the data match conclusions of the manuscript, and the studies are well-conducted and well-described.'

results.result: Chol-MCT1-siRNA, which targets all hepatic cell types including stellate cells, decreased liver collagen 1 levels in genetically obese NASH mouse models. This pan-hepatic MCT1 silencing significantly reduced collagen 1 protein expression in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 1 states 'Novel findings include that deletion of hepatocyte MCT1 does not change liver lipid content, but increases liver fibrosis' and notes that 'concomitant HSC MCT1 deletion does reverse fibrosis seen with hepatocyte MCT1 knockout or knockdown,' implicitly accepting the Chol-siRNA results. The editor describes the manuscript as 'convincing.'

results.result: Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion unexpectedly increased collagen 1 expression and fibrosis. This was observed using both GN-MCT1-siRNA and AAV-TBG-Cre approaches in genetically obese NASH models, with increased collagen 1 at both mRNA and protein levels, enhanced Sirius Red staining, and accelerated liver stiffness.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this surprising finding. Reviewer 1 states 'Novel findings include that deletion of hepatocyte MCT1 does not change liver lipid content, but increases liver fibrosis.' Reviewer 3 notes 'why does decreasing MCT1 expression in hepatocytes exacerbate disease, while silencing MCT1 in fibroblasts seems to alleviate collagen deposition?' indicating acceptance of the finding while questioning mechanism. The editor describes the manuscript as 'convincing.'

results.result: Cell-type-specific targeting tools were developed and validated: GN-MCT1-siRNA selectively silenced MCT1 in hepatocytes only, while Chol-MCT1-siRNA silenced MCT1 in all hepatic cell types, and AAV9-Lrat-Cre achieved hepatic stellate cell-selective MCT1 knockout without affecting hepatocytes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express significant concerns about validation. Reviewer 1 states 'These tools were validated to an extent by the authors, but not sufficiently to ensure that there is no cross-reactivity with other liver cell types' and notes 'other liver cell types should be assessed to ensure specificity' including 'endothelial, cholangiocytes, immune cells.' The editor notes 'future studies are required to validate these new tools.' While the basic functionality is accepted, complete specificity remains uncertain.

results.result: MCT1 depletion in liver (either hepatocyte-specific or pan-hepatic) did not significantly reduce hepatic triglyceride accumulation or resolve steatosis in NASH mouse models, despite effects on de novo lipogenesis gene expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'Novel findings include that deletion of hepatocyte MCT1 does not change liver lipid content' and notes the studies are 'well-conducted and well-described.' The lack of effect on steatosis is acknowledged as distinct from the fibrosis phenotypes.

results.result: Hepatic MCT1 depletion decreased expression of lipogenic transcription factors SREBP1 and ChREBP and their target de novo lipogenesis genes, while increasing AMPK phosphorylation in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these mechanistic findings. Reviewer 2 notes 'The authors have sufficiently addressed prior comments and added new experiments to provide details on possible mechanisms,' suggesting acceptance of the lipogenic pathway data. These findings are treated as supporting evidence for the metabolic effects of MCT1.

results.result: MCT1 depletion in the liver did not cause a surge in plasma lactate levels in ob/ob mice on GAN diet, addressing concerns about potential lactic acidosis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes this finding, stating 'In both models, plasma lactate levels do not change, suggesting that liver MCT1 does not substantially affect systemic lactate.' This is accepted as an important safety observation.

results.result: In LX2 stellate cells, lactate alone did not induce collagen expression, but the combination of lactate and pyruvate enhanced TGF-β1-induced collagen 1 production. MCT1 depletion prevented this TGF-β1-stimulated collagen production regardless of whether lactate was endogenously generated or exogenously supplied.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'Even with the added in vitro data (Figure 8, Supplementary Figure 6), however, a clear mechanistic explanation for how MCT1 is modulating/inhibiting fibrosis in hepatic stellate cells is lacking.' While the data showing lactate potentiation of TGF-β1 is acknowledged ('The authors provide interesting follow up experiments that suggest lactate can potentiate TGF-β1 signaling'), the mechanism remains unclear, particularly regarding 'how intracellular versus extracellular lactate is signaling.'

results.result: MCT1 depletion decreased phosphorylated SMAD3 levels in LX2 cells without TGF-β1 treatment, but this effect was limited with TGF-β1 pretreatment, suggesting both SMAD3-dependent and independent pathways may be involved in MCT1's regulation of collagen production.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'MCT1 depletion decreased the pSMAD3/SMAD ratio, but this was overcome with higher doses of TGB-β1 ligand,' acknowledging the data but expressing that 'a clear mechanistic explanation for how MCT1 is modulating/inhibiting fibrosis in hepatic stellate cells is lacking.' The SMAD3 data is accepted but its mechanistic significance remains uncertain.

results.result: MCT1 depletion in HepG2 hepatocyte cells increased fibrogenic gene markers ACTA2 and COL1A1, but conditioned media from these cells did not affect fibrogenic gene expression in LX2 stellate cells, suggesting a direct cell-autonomous effect in hepatocytes rather than a paracrine effect.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. Reviewer 3's statement that 'the paper opens more questions than it answers: why does decreasing MCT1 expression in hepatocytes exacerbate disease' implicitly accepts the hepatocyte data while questioning mechanism. The conditioned media experiment is accepted as evidence against paracrine signaling.

results.result: Dual MCT1 knockout in both hepatocytes and hepatic stellate cells blunted the individual effects seen in single knockouts, showing no significant change in overall fibrosis compared to control.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as it is consistent with the opposing effects in individual cell types. Reviewer 1 notes 'concomitant HSC MCT1 deletion does reverse fibrosis seen with hepatocyte MCT1 knockout or knockdown,' which aligns with the dual knockout showing intermediate phenotype.

results.result: The opposite fibrotic phenotypes caused by hepatocyte-selective versus pan-hepatic MCT1 silencing were not due to differences in M1/M2 macrophage polarization, as both treatments caused comparable macrophage activation levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. It is accepted as ruling out one potential mechanism for the differential effects, though reviewers note that the actual mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Neither Chol-MCT1-siRNA nor hepatocyte-specific MCT1 knockout improved glucose tolerance in NASH or NAFLD mouse models.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. It is accepted as part of the metabolic characterization showing that MCT1 effects are specific to fibrosis rather than glucose homeostasis in these models.

results.result: The mechanism by which MCT1 affects collagen production differs between cell types: stellate cell MCT1 knockout affected only collagen protein levels (suggesting effects on translation or turnover), while hepatocyte MCT1 knockout affected both mRNA and protein. Increased lactate import into stellate cells may serve as a precursor for collagen amino acid synthesis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'a clear mechanistic explanation for how MCT1 is modulating/inhibiting fibrosis in hepatic stellate cells is lacking' and notes 'It is unclear if upstream/downstream metabolic flux within different cell types leads to fibrotic outcomes.' The differential effects on mRNA versus protein are acknowledged but the mechanistic interpretation remains speculative. Reviewer 1 notes 'Further work would be necessary to dissect mechanism of fibrosis with hepatocyte MCT1.'

results.result: The study concludes that hepatic stellate cell MCT1 is a potential therapeutic target for NASH fibrosis, but this is complicated by the finding that hepatocyte MCT1 depletion increases fibrosis, highlighting the importance of cell-type specificity in therapeutic strategies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this conclusion. The editor states the manuscript represents 'a valuable advance in understanding the role of MCT1' in different liver cell types. Reviewer 3 notes 'The work highlights the complexity of cellular behavior and metabolism within a disease environment,' which aligns with the authors' conclusion about cell-type specificity. However, reviewers emphasize that practical therapeutic application requires better mechanistic understanding.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate in vitro stellate cell data (C6, C51-C54) and stellate cell-specific knockout effects (C4-C5, C95, C98) as supported. OpenEval rates all claims as SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers also find this a 'major finding' but note the stellate cell knockout showed statistical significance for collagen 1 protein but only a trend for trichrome staining. OpenEval separately addresses this discrepancy as UNCERTAIN in R5, while peer reviewers group all stellate cell findings together as SUPPORTED.

Perfect agreement on Chol-siRNA reducing collagen in vivo (C9, C80, C131-C132). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the consistency with in vitro data and appropriate validation, while peer reviewers accept this finding without challenge as part of the broader narrative.

Strong agreement on the surprising pro-fibrotic effect of hepatocyte MCT1 depletion (C10-C11, C82-C84, C130). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes consistency across two methods and models, while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as a 'novel finding' but question the mechanism. OpenEval R6 addresses additional hepatocyte knockout data (C94, C97, C100, C124) that peer reviewers include in the same evaluation.

Partial overlap on stellate cell-specific knockout (C4-C5, C88-C90, C95, C98). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to discrepancy between collagen 1 protein (significant) and trichrome staining (trend only), while peer reviewers group this with other stellate cell data and rate as SUPPORTED overall, describing it as a 'major finding.' This represents a key difference in how the statistical limitations are weighted.

Both address validation of cell-type-specific targeting tools (C55-C63 for siRNA, C88-C89 for AAV). OpenEval rates validation as SUPPORTED with emphasis on rigorous methodological development. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating tools were 'validated to an extent, but not sufficiently to ensure that there is no cross-reactivity with other liver cell types' and requesting assessment of endothelial, cholangiocyte, and immune cells. This is a significant disagreement on validation sufficiency.

Perfect agreement on dual knockout producing intermediate phenotype (C96, C99). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes internal consistency with opposing cell-type-specific effects, while peer reviewers note this aligns with the finding that 'concomitant HSC MCT1 deletion does reverse fibrosis seen with hepatocyte MCT1 knockout.'

Strong agreement on lack of effect on steatosis (C72, C93, C136, C139). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this negative result is important and well-documented across models, while peer reviewers explicitly state 'deletion of hepatocyte MCT1 does not change liver lipid content' and accept this as distinct from fibrosis phenotypes.

Perfect agreement on lipogenic pathway downregulation (C75-C76, C79, C135, C141). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these molecular changes didn't translate to reduced steatosis, suggesting compensatory mechanisms. Peer reviewers note 'authors have sufficiently addressed prior comments and added new experiments to provide details on possible mechanisms.'

Both address lactate potentiation mechanism (C103-C108, C121) but with different confidence levels. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing appropriate experimental design with dose-response and combination treatments. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating 'a clear mechanistic explanation for how MCT1 is modulating/inhibiting fibrosis in hepatic stellate cells is lacking' and noting uncertainty about 'how intracellular versus extracellular lactate is signaling.' Significant disagreement on mechanistic clarity.

Perfect agreement on SMAD3 signaling complexity (C109-C113). Both evaluate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes concentration-dependent effects and that relative contributions of SMAD3-dependent and independent pathways remain unclear. Peer reviewers acknowledge the data but state 'a clear mechanistic explanation for how MCT1 is modulating/inhibiting fibrosis in hepatic stellate cells is lacking.'

Strong agreement on hepatocyte cell-autonomous effects (C115-C118). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the conditioned media experiment appropriately rules out secreted factors. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this data while questioning the broader mechanism of why hepatocyte MCT1 depletion exacerbates disease.

Perfect agreement on macrophage polarization (C86-C87). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this negative result appropriately rules out this alternative mechanism. Peer reviewers accept this finding as part of ruling out potential mechanisms, though note the actual mechanism remains unclear.

Strong agreement on absence of lactic acidosis (C68). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes this addresses a key safety concern. Peer reviewers explicitly note 'plasma lactate levels do not change, suggesting that liver MCT1 does not substantially affect systemic lactate' and accept this as an important safety observation.

Perfect agreement on glucose tolerance (C71). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this negative result is important for understanding metabolic consequences and suggests MCT1's effects on fibrosis are independent of glucose homeostasis. Peer reviewers accept this as part of metabolic characterization showing specificity to fibrosis.

Strong agreement on major conclusions about cell-type-specific effects (C13-C14, C120, C143-C145). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the conclusion is appropriately cautious and represents an important conceptual advance. Peer reviewers state the manuscript represents 'a valuable advance in understanding the role of MCT1' and note 'The work highlights the complexity of cellular behavior and metabolism,' though emphasize practical therapeutic application requires better mechanistic understanding.

Partial overlap on hepatocyte MCT1 knockout worsening fibrosis. OpenEval R6 addresses AAV-TBG-Cre data (C94, C97, C100, C124) as SUPPORTED with convergent evidence from multiple measures. Peer R3 addresses both siRNA and AAV approaches (C10-C11, C82-C84, C94, C97, C100, C124, C130) together as SUPPORTED. Both accept the finding but peer reviewers emphasize the mechanistic questions it raises.

OpenEval identifies differential metabolic effects between siRNA approaches (C69-C70) as SUPPORTED but notes mechanism unexplored. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific claims about differential metabolic effects.

OpenEval documents absence of effects on basic metabolic parameters and liver injury markers in CDHFD model (C92, C102) as SUPPORTED, noting these are important controls for specificity. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressing these control parameters.

OpenEval addresses temporal dynamics of liver stiffness (C101) as SUPPORTED but notes difficulty interpreting discrepancy between early stiffness differences and persistent histological changes. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressing this temporal dynamic.

Peer reviewers evaluate overall mechanistic understanding (C125-C129) as UNCERTAIN, stating 'a clear mechanistic explanation for how MCT1 is modulating/inhibiting fibrosis in hepatic stellate cells is lacking' and noting uncertainty about metabolic flux. OpenEval addresses individual mechanistic components separately (R10 on lactate, R11 on SMAD3, R12 on hepatocyte effects) but does not have a single result evaluating the overall mechanistic picture as uncertain.
